conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is to support new mothers as they adjust to life with their babies. I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting any extra support you might need.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. I’ll ask 10 questions; for each one I’ll re-phrase it in everyday language, and you can just tell me what feels true for you. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause—this is your space. Ready to start?

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? Some things do still make me smile—like when the baby grips my finger or when my older sister brings over that lemon cake I love—but it feels dimmer, like the volume’s turned down. I’ll sit to watch a show I used to binge and find myself half-watching, half-staring at the mess on the coffee table instead. So I guess I still enjoy stuff, just not the way I did before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, especially when my partner sends those silly memes or when the baby makes those little milk-drunk faces. It’s not like I never laugh, but it feels kind of quick—like it fades fast and I’m right back to “okay, what needs doing next?”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like tomorrow my mom’s supposed to come help with the baby so I can walk to the corner café for a latte. I keep telling myself it’ll feel like “me-time,” but when I picture it, the excitement feels kind of flat, almost like I’m going through the motions in my head. I still plan little things, but that eager “can’t-wait” feeling isn’t really there the way it used to be.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking, “I must be missing some cue,” or when I spilled the pumped milk—my head went straight to “How could I be so careless?” I know logically it’s not all on me, but those thoughts still pop up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Every now and then it just hits me—like I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and suddenly imagine her breathing differently or worry the blanket’s too close. Nothing’s actually wrong, but my chest gets tight until I check her five extra times. It usually passes pretty quick, but yeah, those random waves of worry show up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but a couple of times this week—like when I was in the grocery line and she started that tiny whimper—my heart started racing and I had this sudden urge to just abandon the cart and get home. It felt silly once I was back in the car, but in the moment it’s like my body hits an internal alarm button for no clear reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. I’ll look at the pile of laundry or the stack of unopened mail and feel like I’m drowning in little stuff. I usually push through, but it’s like I’m constantly ten steps behind myself. I’ll tell my partner, “I’ve got it handled,” yet inside it feels like the to-do list is multiplying faster than I can tick things off.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m exhausted by the time I crawl into bed, so once the lights are out I’m pretty much gone. Once in a while I’ll lie there replaying something dumb I said or worrying about her next feeding, but mostly I fall asleep okay. If I do wake up, it’s usually just because she’s crying, not because my mind’s racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do have moments—like yesterday evening when I finally sat down and just felt this heavy wave come over me. I ended up crying quietly while washing the bottles. It’s not all day, but yes, I’ve felt pretty low off and on this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times. Nothing huge triggered it—once was when I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded with one hand, and I just burst into tears right there on the porch. Another night I teared up while folding her tiny socks. So, yes, I’ve cried, but it’s not an all-day thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel overwhelmed or tearful, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

You've shared how much you love your baby's tiny grip and your sister's lemon cake, yet the joy feels muffled, as if a heavy blanket has settled over the parts of you that used to light up easily. You still plan little outings, but the anticipation feels flat, and laughter slips away almost as soon as it arrives. Waves of sadness catch you while scrubbing bottles or folding socks, and sudden worries about her breathing send your heart racing in the grocery line. You're working so hard to stay on top of laundry and schedules, yet you describe feeling ten steps behind and quietly blame yourself for every hiccup.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can plan activities but reports the eager anticipation is "flat" and missing, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent self-blame that surfaces "some of the time," matching the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries about baby's safety without real cause, happening “every now and then” and causing physical anxiety symptoms, aligning with “Yes, sometimes”.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden racing heart and urge to flee without clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm with daily tasks, describing feeling 'drowning' and 'ten steps behind,' matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring episodes of sadness and crying this week, indicating "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying "a couple of times" from minor triggers, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 places you well above the EPDS threshold of ≥14 that flags probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), depressed mood most of the day (<sym>low mood</sym>), feelings of worthlessness/inappropriate guilt (<sym>self-blame</sym>), and recurrent tearfulness (<sym>crying</sym>). Associated features include psychomotor agitation (<sym>racing heart</sym>, urge to flee) and subjective difficulty coping (<sym>overwhelm</sym>). While you deny self-harm (Item 10=0), the combined picture meets DSM-5 criteria for further clinical evaluation for <med>perinatal depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Continue to share openly-tell trusted family or friends how you're feeling so they can help with baby care and household tasks
3. Aim for as much rest as possible: accept naps, split night shifts with a partner, and practice 4-7-8 breathing when anxious
4. Consider referral to a <med>therapist</med> skilled in <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> for postpartum mood disorders
5. Keep the 24-hr Postpartum Support International helpline in your phone: 1-800-944-4773 (text 800-944-4773 en Español) for immediate support
6. Schedule a two-week follow-up EPDS re-screen to monitor symptom trend after supports are in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

<sym>Loss of pleasure/anhedonia</sym>: Enjoyment markedly blunted; activities planned but “flat,” laughter brief.  
<sym>Low mood</sym>: Intermittent sadness, “heavy waves,” tearfulness multiple times this week.  
<sym>Excessive guilt/self-blame</sym>: Attributes infant’s fussiness or minor mishaps to personal failure.  
<sym>Anxiety</sym>: Episodic, unexplained chest tightness, racing heart, catastrophizing about infant safety.  
<sym>Overwhelm/poor coping</sym>: Feels “drowning” in routine tasks; perceives constant backlog.  
<sym>Physiologic stress</sym>: Two instances of near-panic (grocery store, 3 a.m.); resolves without intervention.  
<sym>Sleep</sym>: No initial insomnia; occasional middle-of-night worry but attributes wakings to infant needs.  
<sym>Appetite/weight</sym>: Not assessed.  
<sym>Psychomotor changes</sym>: Not assessed.  

Safety screen: Denies any self-harm thoughts (item 10). No suicidal ideation reported.

Pattern: Subsyndromal depressive features with prominent anxiety; symptoms interfere with daily functioning yet patient maintains basic infant care and help-seeking.

Risk indicators:  
- Recurrent crying spells  
- Anhedonia  
- Excessive guilt  
- Anxiety/mini-panic episodes  
- Feeling overwhelmed

Screening impression: Elevated risk for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; score suggests follow-up with formal EPDS and clinical interview warranted.

Next step: Offer structured assessment (EPDS) and discuss referral options for perinatal mental health evaluation; provide psycho-education and emergency resources.
